about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This document is a GAO report to congressional committees on DOD's overseas master plans and the master planning effort for the military buildup on Guam, covering the timeliness of overseas planning reports and factors affecting the Guam plan.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: The fiscal year 2009 overseas master plans generally reflect recent changes in U.S. basing strategies and challenges, and address most prior recommendations, but were submitted 3 months late. The U.S. Pacific Command plan does not describe the Air Force's training challenges in South Korea. DOD has established a framework for the military buildup on Guam but has not issued the congressionally required comprehensive master plan, initially due December 2006 and extended to September 2008; a working-level plan is being developed, but a final master plan is expected no sooner than 2010 after the environmental impact statement and record of decision are completed.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: About 8,000 Marines and 9,000 dependents moving from Okinawa to Guam by 2014. Guam's current population 171,000, increase by 25,000 active duty military personnel and dependents (14.6 percent) to 196,000. Total cost of all services' realignments on Guam estimated over $13 billion; Marine Corps buildup estimated $10.3 billion; Marine Forces Pacific estimate exceeds $15 billion. Government of Japan expected to contribute total $6.09 billion, up to $2.8 billion in funds without reimbursement and $3.3 billion in loans and equity investments. Fiscal year 2009 military construction budget submission approximately $24.4 billion, nearly $1.1 billion (4.7 percent) for overseas. $284 million in facility requirements for ballistic missile defense in Czech Republic. U.S. Central Command host nation funding goal $1.7 billion. Residual value received approximately $656 million since 1989. Koon-Ni training range closed August 2005. Plans submitted April 27 (FY07), March 28 (FY08), mid-May (FY09), 3 months after budget submission. Environmental impact statement expected December 2009, record of decision January 2010; master plan within 90 days after record of decision. Marine Corps realignment cost $2 billion for training ranges; $88 million annually for strategic lift from Guam. DOD requires 500 defense civilians and contractors. Annual construction capacity estimate $1 billion to $1.5 billion, potentially $2.5 billion; DOD needs over $3 billion per year. 15,000 to 20,000 construction workers required; Guam may meet 10 to 15 percent locally. Guam government needs $6.1 billion for infrastructure. Population growth could increase water and wastewater demand by at least 25 percent.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The document recommends that the Secretary of Defense take two actions: (1) Direct the Under Secretary of Defense for Acquisition, Technology and Logistics to initiate a process of developing global defense posture updates earlier each year so that DOD can provide the congressional defense committees the overseas planning report with the administration's annual budget submission; (2) Direct the Executive Director of the Joint Guam Program Office to provide the congressional defense committees with annual updates of the Guam working-level plan until a comprehensive master plan is finalized and submitted to Congress.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The document notes that DOD has not identified all funding requirements for the Guam buildup; plans for force composition, facility requirements, and realignment implications continue to be refined; the environmental impact statement and record of decision are not completed; and there are uncertainties in cost-sharing with Japan. It also notes that overseas master plans may be replaced by global defense posture updates, and that the Guam working-level plan is a onetime snapshot, not a comprehensive master plan. It states that Congress may have limited data on funding requirements without a comprehensive plan.

audience.name: Who it is for
audience.text: This report is addressed to the congressional defense committees, in support of their oversight and funding decisions.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This GAO report, issued August 28, 2008, examines the fate of exported used electronics from the United States, the effectiveness of regulatory controls over these exports, and opportunities for strengthening the federal role in regulating them. It focuses on the Environmental Protection Agency's (EPA) need to better control harmful U.S. exports through stronger enforcement of its cathode-ray tube (CRT) rule and more comprehensive regulation of other used electronics.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: The report finds that while some exported used electronics are handled responsibly, a substantial amount ends up in developing countries where they are often handled and disposed of unsafely. It finds that current U.S. regulatory controls do little to stem the export of potentially hazardous used electronics because the scope of regulatory control is narrow (only CRTs are regulated as hazardous waste), regulatory controls are easily circumvented, and EPA has done little to enforce the CRT rule. The report also finds that EPA has several options to strengthen the federal role, including amending RCRA regulations, submitting a legislative package for Basel Convention ratification, cooperating with other agencies to improve tracking, and updating RCRA regulations to reflect OECD changes.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: Americans removed more than 300 million electronic devices from their households in 2006. CRTs contain 4 pounds of lead. EPA can seek criminal penalties of up to $50,000 per day of violation and imprisonment of up to 2 years. Hong Kong intercepted and returned 26 shipping containers of used CRT monitors since January 2007. GAO found 43 electronics recyclers willing to export broken, untested, or nonworking CRTs. Three other companies indicated they do not export broken CRTs, and 7 others asked for more information. EPA records show that none of the recyclers willing to sell to us had filed proper notifications. At least 3 of these companies held Earth Day 2008 electronics-recycling events. As of June 2008, 25 companies submitted 47 notices for export of CRTs for recycling. As of July 2008, only 1 of the 43 companies submitted a notification for recycling. A United Nations University study found that the manufacturing phase takes up 80 percent of the natural resources used during the life cycle of computers. The U.S. Geological Survey reports that 1 metric ton of computer scrap contains more gold than 17 metric tons of ore. Samsung Corning's contractor ships about 250 shipping containers, totaling about 4,000 tons of CRT glass, leave the United States for the Malaysian facility each month. Over 95 percent of the electronic items that Umicore recycles become new electronic products. In a search of one Internet e-commerce site, we observed brokers place 2,234 requests to purchase LCD screens, 430 requests for central processing units, and 665 requests for used computers. In an extensive search over 3 months, we observed brokers make 230 requests for about 7.5 million used CRTs. Over 75 percent of the brokers' requests offered $10 or less per unit, and almost half offered $5 or less. About 70 percent of the requests came from developing countries in Asia. A study published in 2007 found that children in Guiyu had lead levels in their blood that were more than 50 percent higher than the limit set by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Scavengers in Cambodia collect material for as little as $1 a day. Shipping rates to West Africa range from $4,000 to $7,000 per 20-foot container, compared to $750 to ship 40-foot containers to Hong Kong. One African computer importer said he can still make a profit if he receives a shipment of up to 40 percent 'junk.' EPA issued its first administrative penalty complaint in July 2008, seeking the maximum civil penalty of $32,500. EPA reported having 10 ongoing investigations, 7 of which appeared to be from us. A New York electronics recycler made four purchases of used electronics, including 221 CRT monitors. A Georgia electronics recycler purchased two lots of computer monitors, one lot of 100 CRT monitors for $45 and another lot of 155 CRT monitors for $366. This company offered to 'hand stuff' the container for an additional $400 to increase the load from about 850 monitors to between 1,100 and 1,200 monitors per container. EPA submitted proposed changes to RCRA regulations to the Office of Management and Budget on May 8, 2008.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The report recommends that the Administrator, EPA, identify a timetable for developing and implementing a systematic plan to enforce the CRT rule, including enforcement targets, monitoring, follow-up of suspected violations, and prosecution. The report also recommends that the Administrator, EPA, direct the heads of appropriate offices to: develop options on how the agency could broaden its regulations under existing RCRA authority to address the export of used electronic devices that might not be classified as hazardous waste but have a high likelihood of threatening human health and the environment when unsafely disassembled (including expanding the scope of the CRT rule and revising the regulatory definition of hazardous waste); and cooperate with other federal agencies to improve the tracking of exported used electronics, which could be accomplished by implementing specific harmonized tariff codes for these devices. In addition, because determining whether to ratify international treaties rests with Congress and the President, the report recommends that EPA submit to Congress a legislative package for ratification of the Basel Convention.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The report notes that EPA has not yet updated its RCRA regulations to reflect the 2001 OECD decision, and although EPA officials anticipate issuing a proposed rule in mid-November, the outcome is pending. The report also notes that the outcome of EPA's investigation into containers of CRT monitors was pending at the time of the report. EPA disagreed with the report's recommendations, preferring nonregulatory, voluntary approaches, but the report states that nothing in EPA's comments changes the reality that the United States' regulatory coverage of exported used electronics is among the narrowest in the industrialized world and that the little regulation that does exist has been enforced to only a minor degree.

audience.name: Who it is for
audience.text: The report is addressed to the Committee on Foreign Affairs, House of Representatives, to support its oversight of EPA's regulation and enforcement of U.S. exports of used electronics.
